Presenter script

Find My Ride examines a narrow but stressful moment: after booking, the app can show a pin, or even say the driver has arrived, while rider and driver still cannot find each other. The goal is to understand when coordination breaks and what Uber should test first.

Presenter script

A word on method. Synchronous interviews were not feasible, so I built a multilingual self-serve app with rider and driver branches and optional open-text or voice prompts. After removing one duplicate, the base is sixty-two respondents: fifty-eight riders and four drivers. Thirty answered open-ended questions and eleven wrote extended accounts. This gave breadth and language coverage, but no live probing, so it does not replace moderated interviews.

text:
Presenter script

Desk research changed the framing. Uber already publishes Hyderabad airport guidance, including in-app directions and the D1 pickup zone. Grab, Lyft, Waymo, and MyGate show patterns for venue guidance, structured handoffs, and access-aware stops. These are design precedents, not proof of local value. The opportunity is better coverage, clarity, and recovery within real access and stopping constraints.

text:
Presenter script

A credible market estimate needs Hyderabad four-wheel pickup volume, the share starting at complex locations, and the share experiencing material difficulty. Those inputs are not publicly available, so I show the model and exposure pools rather than inventing a TAM. Public sources show large passenger flows at the airport, metro, and railway stations. For this problem, location type is more useful than demographic segmentation.

text:
Presenter script

The research goal is to understand what breaks during difficult pickups and how people recover. The evidence points to a shared-reference-point problem at complex locations, not proof that the map is always wrong. The rider is the primary user, with the driver as the connected stakeholder. The job statement remains an assumption to validate. Success would mean fewer reactive contacts and lower arrived-to-trip-start dwell.

Presenter script

The sample says the problem is meaningful, but not universal. Twenty-four of fifty-one recent four-wheel users reported difficulty or uncertainty. Among twenty-eight issue cases, twenty-three said the problem had happened before, twenty said calls or messages helped, and six said nothing helped. “Happened before” does not prove the same venue repeatedly failed, and these percentages are not Hyderabad-wide prevalence.

text:
Presenter script

The cases concentrate in complex places: airports, gated residences, malls, offices, and stations. Calling is the dominant recovery action, followed by waiting and moving. The app often hands the final physical coordination step back to rider and driver. The opportunity is to reduce that manual effort. The appendix lists all ten insights and their evidence strength.

text:
Presenter script

The recommended direction is to make the fallback faster without making the map more complicated. P-zero is a structured meeting note. P-one is guided recovery when coordination stalls. P-two is reusable venue information. This is a test sequence, not a committed roadmap, and it should appear only at selected complex locations.

Presenter script

The strongest first test is a structured pre-arrival meeting note. At flagged complex pickups, ask for one concise handoff: gate or side, landmark, and waiting spot. One respondent already does this manually. Test whether the prompt reduces reactive calls, arrived-to-trip-start dwell, location changes, and cancellations without adding friction to normal pickups.

Presenter script

P-one is guided stalled-pickup recovery. Start with reconnect actions, and test reassignment only for unresolved cases because it affects driver time and marketplace cost. P-two is venue-specific coordination information at two or three validated venues. That requires ownership and expiry because stale access guidance can be worse than no guidance.

Presenter script

My recommendation is to test the smallest coordination aid first, not commit to a broad build. The evidence is limited: asynchronous research without live probing, only four drivers, and a non-representative sample. The highest-value next step is moderated rider and driver research, plus reliable arrived-to-trip-start data at selected venues. The appendix and evidence ZIP carry full traceability.
